t: Minimum Cost to Separate Sentence Into Rows — DP Over Word Boundaries
o: Break a space-separated sentence into rows of at most k characters: word order is fixed, words never split, and words inside a row are joined by single spaces. A row of length n costs (k - n)^2 unless it is the last row, which is free. Example 1 ("i love leetcode", k = 12): "i love" + "leetcode" costs (12-6)^2 = 36, beating one-word-per-row at 121 + 64 = 185; "love leetcode" is impossible at length 13 > 12. In Example 2 (k = 7) the optimal packing pays 1 + 16 + 0 + 4 = 21, and Example 3 shows a single-row sentence costs 0 because the only row is free. Since rows partition the word sequence in order and a row's feasibility depends only on which words it spans, the problem has optimal substructure over boundaries between words — classic dynamic programming. Each extra word adds at least 2 characters, so any candidate row holds O(k) words, keeping transitions short.
k: State on word boundaries: 'the first i words are already placed' summarizes everything the future needs.
The final row is FREE — either keep its cost out of the recurrence or subtract it at the end; mixing this up is the classic bug.
Row length for words i..j is pref[j+1] - pref[i] + (j - i): prefix sums of word lengths make each check O(1).
Greedy maximal packing is NOT optimal — ending a row early can shrink squared slack later, so dynamic programming is required.

a.n: Approach 1: Top-Down Memoized DP (Last Row Free)
a.i: Define dp(i) as the minimum cost of laying out words i..n-1 where the row STARTING at i is treated as the last row and is therefore free, while every later row is charged. Try every first-row endpoint j whose row fits within k; if it consumes all remaining words it contributes 0, otherwise it contributes (k - length)^2 plus dp(j+1). Memoize over i.
s: dp(i): extend the current row word by word, tracking running length; stop once length exceeds k.
A row reaching the last word contributes 0; otherwise contribute (k - length)^2 + dp(next).
Take the minimum over feasible endpoints and memoize.
a.t: O(m · min(m, k)) — each boundary extends its row at most about k/2 words before overflowing k columns.
a.sp: O(m) — memoization table plus recursion depth.

a.n: Approach 2: Bottom-Up Tabulation with Explicit Last-Row Pass
a.i: Charge EVERY completed row during the DP: dp[i] = minimum cost of packing the first i words into full rows. Transition dp[i] = min over previous boundary j of dp[j] + (k - len(row j..i-1))^2 whenever the row fits. Because the true last row must be free, finish by scanning every boundary j whose remaining suffix fits in one row and taking the smallest dp[j].
s: Build prefix sums of word lengths.
dp[0] = 0; everything else starts at infinity.
For each i, walk j backwards from i-1 while the row j+1..i still fits in k columns, relaxing dp[i] with dp[j] + slack^2.
Scan every j such that words j..n-1 fit in one row and take the minimum dp[j].
a.t: O(m · min(m, k)) — backwards extension stops after roughly k/2 words since each adds at least two characters.
a.sp: O(m) — prefix sums and the dp array.

w: Lead with the top-down version in an interview — the state and transition read directly off the statement — then mention tabulation as an implementation choice. Pitfalls: charging the free last row (answer inflated by its squared slack), dropping the single inter-word space from row length, and trusting greedy packing (construct cases where breaking early wins). Edge cases: one-word sentences (cost 0), k exactly equal to some word length, sentences forcing one word per row. Follow-ups: linear instead of quadratic slack (same DP), or minimizing the number of rows first (BFS over boundaries).
